matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: Yongwen mubiao”蔣公用文墓表 [1424], in Yang's Dongli wenji 東里文集 [1440] 16.20b-22b. 71 Yang's preface to Yuji weiji 玉機微義 ended by praising Chen Yi for diffusing medical teachings, as medicine was “the art by which the sages display benevolence upon the people” (醫者聖人仁民之術也; LiuChYQ: 73). History of the Ming (138: 4137) indicates that in the early Zhengtong reign (in or soon after 1436), Yang “dispatched military and civil officials to zhenfu Jiangxi, Huguang, Henan, and Shandong” (分遣文武鎮撫江西湖廣 河南 山東). Yang was probably the one who sent Chen to Shaanxi in 1435. John Dardess (1996: 179-89) discussed Yang's patronizing of natives of Taihe, but said little about his relations with other court officials. 72 LiuChYQ: 463. In 1438 Yang Shiqi had been named Junior Preceptor (少師), a prestige title ranked 1b. Duxian 都憲 is not listed in Hucker 1985, but it probably referred to a post in the Censorate. A sample mistake in Chen's edition: “Wang Andao” 王安道 (Zhu's disciple Wang Liu) was turned into “Yu'an daoren” 玉安道人 (“Taoist master Yu'an”; juan 1, “Wind strokes,” “neiyin si zhongfeng lun” 内因似中風論; LiuChYQ: 117A). 73 Angela Leung (2003b: 132) postulated that Yang's writing a preface for it showed that the Yijing xianxue 醫經小學 was “an important introductory textbook during the early Ming,” but it appears that Yang's preface enabled rather than recognized the influence of this text.
